title: He loved us (Dilexit Nos, 2024)
hook: Francis's last encyclical returns to the Sacred Heart
tomorrow: who was really holding the pen when Paul wrote?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a letter that skipped the greeting: Christ is alive, and he wants you alive. He is alive, present tense.

"Love you" at the end of a phone call is present tense. Hang up with "loved you" and it would sound like a breakup. So here's a strange title. Pope Francis wrote an encyclical on the Sacred Heart of Jesus, and named it with two Latin words: Dilexit nos. He loved us. Past tense. Why would a letter about love that's still going pick a verb that sounds finished?
screen: `LOVE YOU, NOT LOVED YOU.` → `DILEXIT NOS.` → `WHY THE PAST TENSE?`

segments.voice: The answer is in Paul. In his letter to the Romans, he runs through everything that might cut a person off from Christ: trouble, distress, hunger, danger, persecution, the sword. Then he answers the list, in the Douay-Rheims: "But in all these things we overcome, because of him that hath loved us." That's where Francis found his title. Paul isn't describing a love that might happen, if. He's pointing at something already done, and Francis says Paul writes it so we'll see nothing can separate us from that love. Past tense means it can't be taken back. Then Francis slows down over one word: heart. In the Bible, he notes, the heart is the deepest center of a person, beneath appearances, where thoughts and choices take shape. He worries about a world losing its heart, rushing from one thing to the next. Against that, he points to the heart of Christ, a human heart carrying divine love. The letter remembers Margaret Mary Alacoque, a nun in France who, tradition says, saw Christ show her his heart. And it goes back to the cross, where John says a soldier pierced Jesus' side, and blood and water came out. So the puzzle solves itself. A heart that knows it was loved, past tense, settled, can begin to love in return. Francis says the world can begin to change from there.
screen: `TROUBLE, DISTRESS, THE SWORD.` · `BECAUSE OF HIM THAT HATH LOVED US.` · `THE HEART: THE DEEPEST CENTER.` · `BLOOD AND WATER FROM HIS SIDE.` · then, large: `HE LOVED US.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand flat over your heart and feel it beating under your palm. Let three words sit there, he loved us, already given, nothing to earn. If you pray, speak to the heart of Jesus in your own words, or just stay there in silence.
He loved us. Paul's words about Christ, which Francis chose as the name of his letter on the Sacred Heart.
The line to keep: he loved us, past tense, already done and not taken back. Rest well.

howItsDone: Catholics honor the Sacred Heart of Jesus with a feast each year and in images of the Heart at home and in church; Dilexit Nos invites a return to that devotion.

fork.setup: a friend says she can't pray because she hasn't been good enough lately to deserve God's attention. what does the past tense of dilexit nos say to her?
options: get your life in order first, then come back.
the love came first and is already given; she can start from there.

fork.reveal: Paul and Francis point to a love already done, past tense. a heart that knows it was loved can begin to love in return.

chat.says: yelled at my dad. he still drove me to 6am practice like nothing happened. why do i feel worse??
options: Because love that comes first asks for an answer, not payback. Start with a real sorry.
Because now you owe him. Love's a deal, so pay it back with a favor this week.
Because he's secretly still mad. Wait until he brings it up before you apologize.
